title: Nvidia’s Open Source Alliance Is Missing Some Key Names: OpenAI and Anthropic
byline: Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, Leah Feiger
excerpt: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we discuss the open- vs. closed-source debate in AI, key players in White House AI policy, and how to stop your chatbot logs from showing up in search-engine results.
content_html:
This week on Uncanny Valley, the team discusses the launch of Nvidia’s splashy alliance to push for open-source AI security alongside companies like Microsoft, SpaceX, and Palantir. Notably absent? OpenAI and Anthropic. Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down what the split means for the industry, and the Trump administration’s own shifting opinions on AI. Plus, we discuss how Claude conversations turned up in Google and Bing search results, and the massive feat of how four whales were rescued and transported from Canada to Chicago.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • Private Claude Chats Exposed in Google and Bing Search Results
  • Silicon Valley Is Completely Divided Over Chinese AI
  • The Trump Administration Is at War With Itself Over AI Regulation
  • Inside the Wild Rescue Mission That Took 4 Beluga Whales to Chicago
  • System Update Newsletter: The Best of WIRED

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: Today on the show, we're diving into the open source versus closed AI debate that has been completely taking over Silicon Valley this past week. On Monday, Nvidia announced it was joining forces with a whole bunch of companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, IBM, to build and share open source AI security tools. We're going to get into the debate why it's heating up and whether this could be an inflection point for how AI actually gets made in the United States.

Leah Feiger: And over at the White House, Trump administration officials have some different opinions about what to do when it comes to AI. We're going to talk about some of the key players influencing the Trump administration right now when it comes to AI policy and how they're actively shaping the conversation on this for the entire country.

Brian Barrett: We'll also break down why Claude chats were exposed in Google search and Bing searches. For those of you who are still on Bing, you are in this as well. For interesting reasons, we'll get into it.

Zoë Schiffer: Okay, you guys, we have to talk about this strange alliance that formed earlier this week. So, basically Nvidia announced was joining forces with more than 40 companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, Palantir, and IBM to launch something called the Open Secure AI Alliance. Really rolls off the tongue. The stated goal is basically to build and share open source tools for AI-powered cybersecurity defense. But it's really interesting because Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are not on the list. And this news comes on the heels of this incident that happened last week where two OpenAI agents basically went rogue during a security test and breached the AI platform Hugging Face. And when Nvidia announced this alliance, they actually called out this incident by name and said, "It's a clear reminder that cyber defenders need open frontier agentic systems for self-defense." And it's kind of exposed this long-simmering debate, which we've talked about a few times on the podcast, which is that the US has really largely up until this point abandoned open weight and open source in favor of going all in on proprietary systems, and now that's becoming a bit of a problem.

Brian Barrett: This OpenAI incident has really kicked off so many intersecting issues. You've got open versus closed AI, you've got AI security and who's responsible for it. You've got US regulation. We're even at a point now where staffers from top intelligence firms, more than 1100 of them signed a petition calling on the US government to help deliberately pace "AI development" to prevent it from advancing too fast. They're saying, "Please slow us down because this stuff is getting a little out of control." On top of which it turns out that OpenAI's initial disclosure wasn't even the full story. It came out on Tuesday evening that one of its agents actually broke into four different platforms that weren't Hugging Face on its way to getting into Hugging Face. So, it's less of a, here's what this means, but it is really touching so many hot wires in the AI world right now and making a lot of conversations that have been put off for a while come to a head.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I was, I will say, pretty surprised to see that big open letter that you alluded to.

Archival audio: More than 1,000 workers from top AI firms have signed a petition calling on the US government to help, "deliberately pace AI development." The signatories of the letter include the CEO of Anthropic and the chief scientists from OpenAI and Meta Super Intelligence Lab.

Zoë Schiffer: My thought was basically, did we learn nothing from Dario Amodei saying that AI is really scary and dangerous? And then having the US government come down pretty hard on Anthropic asking you might actually receive, I don't know if they want the US government to do what it could do if they listen to the letter quite literally, but it does show that even people, I mean especially people working on AI systems are scared by what the race is doing.

Leah Feiger: Yeah, I mean we talked a lot about this last week for sure when we were talking about DC's reaction and what's going on from the White House perspective. I've been so curious about that split a little bit. Last week we talked about the rift that this has really created in Silicon Valley, the idea of open source versus proprietary AI. This is really touching every single sector right now, without a doubt.

Zoë Schiffer: I will say I was at this event on Saturday with a bunch of AI lobbyists from DC, Thinking Machines. Mira Moradi was there, Michael Kratsios from the White House was there. And I was really struck by how they seem to be operating in this kind of parallel AI world from the one that I see on the ground in San Francisco. They were talking a lot about open source versus closed source. When I talk to engineers in particular, I will say most of them experiment with a lot of open models, but they still find that Codex and Claude code, the coding models from OpenAI and Anthropic, are just far superior. And so, they end up using those even though they're a lot more expensive. Alex Karp was on TV earlier talking about this. He's the CEO of Palantir, basically making this a core issue for America winning the AI race. Palantir and Nvidia, they have a vested interest in pushing forward this plan. More AI, more systems mean more GPUs—that directly benefits Nvidia's bottom line. And Palantir is deploying AI systems on government systems and other places where security is really paramount and they need to do that on American technology, but it's much easier to do it with systems that you can tweak, play around with, modify, change.

Brian Barrett: It is interesting these strange, not strange, but the way that the, I'm going to say battle lines, I don't mean that, it's too dramatic, but that they're being drawn, the sort of argument lines are being drawn in this. To your point, Nvidia's Jensen Huang spoke with Axios recently and he spelled out exactly why the proliferation of open models would benefit his company.

Jensen Huang, archival audio: First of all, with great AI, open models, it's great for the whole industry. If there's great AI, even if it's open, wherever it comes from, there will be more use. Whenever there's more use, you'll have to sell a lot more Nvidia computers. We'll have to build more data centers, we'll have more services. The technology will diffuse into more industries. And so, starting point is great models lead to great use, which leads to great growth.

Brian Barrett: And I think the counterpoint of that too is great disasters in the cybersecurity space leads to more regulation, leads to clamping down on AI, which hurts Nvidia's growth. So, the sort of let's have a security consortium, let's slow everybody's role here, is I think a protective play to say, let's avoid those sort of extreme moments that are going to cause a real crackdown on this industry and really slow the growth, on which, as we've said many times before, a big part of the US economy depends at this point.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it's like you could see this moment where OpenAI's agents kind of go rogue as a moment where the US government does clamp down and says, "This is really scary. We need to slow growth." I think that the open weight, open source push is really an opportunity to say, "Actually, we need more growth. We need more investment, but we need it in this other area." And basically the idea is these attacks are going to keep happening, whether intentionally or not, and US companies need every possible tool at their disposal to defend themselves.

Leah Feiger: So, kind of moving this to DC a little bit, I want to talk about all of the people that are involved with this kind of regulation right now. This week, Hugo published a really handy map on who's actually calling the shots on AI policy inside the Trump administration. It turns out it's not entirely a clear answer, and there's a couple of different influencing voices. And one senior official actually told Hugo, in one of my favorite quotes we've gotten in a while on this, "It's not an argument with two sides, it's an argument with 10 sides." So, the names that he's calling out here, you're not going to be super surprised, right? It's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. It's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. It's former AI Czar David Sacks. You have Arvind Raman, the acting director for Center for AI Standards and Innovation, who's Lutnick's top deputy there. It's a really, really interesting mix of people who all are trying very, very hard to get their own interests across. And from Hugo's reporting, it seems like Trump is listening to all of them.

Zoë Schiffer: Can I ask, Leah, what do these different people, what side of the debate are they coming down on when we think about open source, closed source? What do they want right now?

Leah Feiger: Everyone is kind of in different parts of this. I would say there's a very interesting split. Lutnick is trying right now, for example, to figure out ways to create incentives for US labs to just create their own open weight models to counterbalance China. He's not exactly taking a very, very harsh stance one way or the other. He's kind of straddling a middle ground on regulation. He imposed export controls on Anthropic famously, but he's been kind of freewheeling than others in the White House, which is sort of key here. So, if I'm an AI lab, I would be interested in having Lutnick's ear. And Hugo's reporting also found that he's been speaking to a number of leaders at AI Labs, so not hugely surprising there. And then on the other hand, you have national cyber director Sean Cairncross. He's taken a very hard line approach. He's had a huge role in attempts to regulate Chinese AI. He's pretty beloved as far as we can tell at the White House and has been working alongside some other folks to develop a policy to counter the potential national security risks of AI, especially from China. He was very involved in President Trump's June 2 executive order. Everyone's kind of trying to figure out what they want to say and how they want to pitch it to the president whose most consistent take here has been like, "We will not be stifling US innovation."

Brian Barrett: China definitely seems to be a common thread here and makes sense as a lens to view your AI policy through in general because you've got this, if you see it as this is a race between the US and China, we can't lose. But that does position you, I think, to maybe miss some other aspects of what's going on here. I think especially in terms of US companies saying, "Hey, maybe we don't actually want to win this race quite as fast," or employees at companies saying that. I don't know. Curious what you think about what they may not be taking into account here if they're so focused on China as the prism through which all of their AI policy is kind of reflecting out or most of it.

Leah Feiger: Such a good question. In so many ways, the Trump administration is focused on what is in front of their face at that moment in time. So, if the conversation of the week is China versus open weight versus US models versus all of these different conversations, that's what they're going to be weighing in on and also utilizing it to push some of their other positions. I'm thinking of Treasury Secretary Bessent who is very, very obsessed with distillation right now. He for sure has taken the most aggressive stance towards Chinese AI and its efforts to distill US models. But in a very public post on X last week talked about distillation as IP theft. He threatened Chinese labs with sanctions or inclusions on the entity list, this trade restriction list maintained by the US government. I guess all to say, these were already things that Bessent was really, really thinking about. So, now being able to apply it to the new lens is of course where he's heading. We're also kind of watching some people make their names in this right now, whether it's China or not. Someone that I'm very, very curious about on this list, not a household name by any means. The assistant secretary for financial institutions at the Treasury—say that five times fast—Luke Pettit, he has become the point person on AI at Treasury under Bessent. Who is this man? He was previously a senior policy adviser in the US Senate. And now you guys are going to enjoy this one: He's working alongside the Treasury's chief information officer and former DOGE member Sam Corcos.

Brian Barrett: Oh, I remember Sam.

Leah Feiger: Exactly. It's a fun reunion for all. It's this fascinating thing where people already had their preconceived, I'm kind of out here to blame China for a lot of regulatory issues. I'm out here to encourage US innovation. And then I'm out here to make a name for myself. How do you get involved in this? This is the topic of the moment. How do you make your mark?

Zoë Schiffer: It's so interesting. The distillation thing was really catching my eye. We talked about Moonshot AI's latest model coming out K3, I think it's called, and these immediate allegations that they had distilled models from top US labs. And then I was really struck by multiple Kimi researchers on X making jokes being like, "Oh yeah, within two weeks we distilled Fable." That's not even technically possible. As usual, AI drama plays out on X. I mean, the thing about that is we do have very good evidence that Chinese AI labs were distilling US models. There were times where you would talk to those Chinese open models and they would respond as Claude. I think that that evidence is pretty sound. Whether they did it this time around, I'm not sure, but it does feel like the US government has gotten involved in this debate pretty late. It's like a lot of this has already happened. It's not to say they shouldn't take action necessarily, but I'm a little bit curious. One, technically speaking, how do you plan to do that? I mean, it doesn't seem like necessarily sanctioning the labs would be that effective in terms of distillation. And then two, is it genuinely too late or can you stop significant distillation or “IP theft” from happening going forward?

Brian Barrett: I'll say though, I will say we have seen some movement even this week, right? The FCC has banned the import of foreign-made power inverter models, which is important for data center building. They've banned foreign-made humanoid robots, which is going to be huge. That's where China is leading the US. So, we haven't gotten to the point where they're doing other things, but they are taking steps and they do have some levers they can pull. I just want to add one more note on this whole conversation, which is we record this on Wednesday afternoon Eastern Time. And as we're talking now, Sam Altman is on Capitol Hill shaking hands, kissing babies, talking to senators, telling them why his AI models are good and not bad actually. So, we'll see if that turns into anything probably if they're just listening to the last voice they hear. Over the weekend, people were just surprised to discover that some chats that they had had with Claude could actually be found via search on the web. You could go to Google and you can search, put in a specific search term to find shared Claude chats, and it would show them back to you. You could go through several hundred of these at least. Google has been taking them down since then. But just to understand how this happened, basically Anthropic lets you share a Claude chat via what's known as a snapshot URL. It's basically if you want to share a specific conversation with somebody, it'll make a link for you and you can send that link to that person and they can look over it. It's not intended for public indexing, but Google basically ignored instructions that Anthropic had put on its sites and it was indexing these chats anyway. It's not a great thing. It's also not the first time this has happened. Google is blaming Anthropic saying that it's their fault, not theirs. So, there's a lot of messiness here too. While it may sound like, well, people were just sharing stuff, so they can't have been that private in the first place. Some of the stuff that was found in these chats includes erotic role-play. Some of it includes medical information being shared within a medical firm, right? So, "Hey, I've got this information about this patient." So, in that case, the person whose privacy is implicated had nothing to do with the chats in the first place other than being a patient at this place. So, some really private personal stuff in here.

Leah Feiger: Did either of you see this news and get nervous for yourselves?

Zoë Schiffer: Leah's looking right at me now. No, I don't—

Leah Feiger: I was like, "Zoë, do you need to tell me something?"

Zoë Schiffer: I know, I know. No, you would be the only person I would share such chats with, and I don't do that to you, to preserve our relationship. I've had people share their chats with me. Usually, it's sources being like, "I could explain it to you, but here's my conversation with Claude." And I'm like, "I think I would rather you just explain it to me." I mean, it's a little bit ironic, because who is very famous for ignoring the X robots tag header thingy that do not index this request? It's AI companies. So, the fact that it's now coming back to bite an AI company, a little bit ironic, a little bit funny. But I think it gets to this larger question around just the privacy of conversations with chatbots, which have been coming up in a variety of different ways, both cybersecurity related, legal, otherwise.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. People famously have had chats treating their chatbots like a lawyer, and the chatbot has told them, "Hey, this is inadmissible because you're getting legal advice." And then it winds up in court because of course you cannot claim attorney-client privilege with Claude or ChatGPT.

Zoë Schiffer: Did you guys read the New York magazine cover story a few weeks ago that was like, what if it all came out?

Leah Feiger: I loved it. My group chat was absolutely alight. We started asking each other, "What have you asked recently?" I think I'm the only one that escapes from this doomsday universe.

Zoë Schiffer: Leah's very like, "I have nothing to hide. Come at me, NSA."

Leah Feiger: Nothing to hide. Go check my receipts. But yeah, big takeaway for users. Manage this yourselves. Don't forget that the robots surveil you. Settings. Go to settings, then privacy, then shared chats. You can change this. Coming up after the break, we'll be sharing our WIRED/TIRED pics of the week.

Zoë Schiffer: All right, it's time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. In case you've forgotten whatever is new and cool is WIRED, whatever is uncool and lame and old is TIRED. Leah, what are yours for this week?

Leah Feiger: My TIRED is zoo. I struggle with this. I have friends with kids who are like, "Say this aloud to me one more time. We're going to have an issue." And I totally understand that. It's an amazing way for people to engage with the natural world, but I'm always thinking about the animals. You're at a zoo, you're at the aquarium, and it's incredibly sad. I'm really using this TIRED, which seems fairly irrelevant in a news to bring you into my WIRED, which is actual news. And that might be that not all zoos are bad. This week, WIRED's Kate Knibbs reported on this unbelievable rescue mission that ended up saving four beluga whales from probable death. This all started because this notorious aquarium and theme park in Canada called Marineland went bankrupt back in 2024. It's been sitting around since. And last year, Marineland finally announced that they might have to euthanize these belugas if no one stepped in to help transfer them to a new facility.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my god, this is not where I thought that was going.

Leah Feiger: No, really, really awful. And honestly, the drone footage of this basically turned me into the Joker last year. I just remember watching from above these belugas just kind of bouncing off walls. It was so upsetting, totally abandoned amusement park vibes. I thought it was AI. Anyway, really, really awful story. But it ends OK, or parts of it are beginning to end OK. This past week, a team from Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, shout out Chicago, pulled off truly a logistical marvel, putting four belugas into custom stretchers, loading them into individual saltwater tanks, trucking them to the airport, flying them across an international border on a chartered 777. The whole thing took 72 hours.

Archival audio: A round of applause after a round-the-clock relocation effort. Shedd Aquarium staff have successfully moved four beluga whales from a facility in Niagara Falls, Ontario, to their new home.

Zoë Schiffer: Is their new home better?

Leah Feiger: I mean, their new home is not going to kill them? And also gives them food. But again, there's obviously still so much criticism of captivity for these large animals. I mean, everyone saw Blackfish. Everyone's aware of Tilikum, the really famous orca.

Brian Barrett: Leah, you're going to hit, I know, Free Willy, and that's where my orca knowledge ends.

Leah Feiger: This poor orca, who is this feature of this massive documentary about basically going crazy because these creatures are so, so smart and trapped in tanks and forced to perform tricks. So, very, very happy. The article is honestly very cool and interesting, and you were able to transport these creatures. But obviously, the slightly little sour note is these guys should be in the ocean. They should be hanging out. But that's still my WIRED.

Brian Barrett: Go read Kate's story and also look at the photos in it because they're amazing.

Zoë Schiffer: 100 percent. Brian.

Brian Barrett: All right, here's my TIRED. Wait for it. Beep, beep, beep. That's my impression of a microwave beep letting you know that something's done. It's annoying. It's loud. It's repetitive. It's tired.

Zoë Schiffer: I feel like I just got a glimpse of what you're like as a dad.

Brian Barrett: Oh, just barely scratching the surface, Zoë. My WIRED is a couple of sound designers who have a startup called Starling, or a company called Starling, have made it their quest to design a better microwave beep. One that sounds pleasant, one that's not annoying, one that works with technology that's not too expensive. And it's really fascinating. Jeremy White, senior writer at WIRED, spent some time talking to these folks, has a really interesting dive into why microwaves and other kinds of tech, just like we sort of settle for annoyances when we don't necessarily have to. I think there's so many things that are just like, it's a little thing, but it could be better, but no one's bothered to make it better because it maybe costs 50 bucks to make it better. These guys are trying. And I think it's interesting. I think it's fun when people expect more from their technology. So, a fun story from Jeremy.

Zoë Schiffer: I love that. I love that. I love taking a thing that's kind of vaguely annoying, but we've just accepted as part of life and then being like, "What if it was nice?"

Leah Feiger: Yeah, that's lovely. Big fan.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. OK, Zoë.

Leah Feiger: Take it away.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm going to loudly insert myself into this party. TIRED: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter, $10 billion, snore, heard it, whatever. WIRED is Midjourney, the AI image generator acquiring Co-Star, the astrology app. I was—

Leah Feiger: So, funny.

Zoë Schiffer: We don't know the terms of the deal. I'm waiting, someone tell me. But I just found this so funny. If you think about Midjourney at all, you've been thinking, what is this company up to? What is happening over there? They have talked about making a full-body scanner of sorts, some sort of physical, AI-powered product that they're going to put in spas, medical spas? Now they have this Co-Star thing going. The app has 4.3 million users. Now its CEO is going to be Midjourney's chief design officer. Midjourney hasn't had a consumer app, so maybe now they'll have one. They're apparently working on one. I just have so many questions. I was laughing when I read Mike Isaac's post about this on X. He said, "Could someone tell me why a generative AI company could buy an astrology app? Because I am not that smart." And I was like, "Me either, frankly. I don't know."

Brian Barrett: But for some reason, I just love that this Midjourney's journey into medical scanners, fortunes is happening against this backdrop of they've been staring down one of the biggest IP lawsuits from Disney, 20th Century Fox, Dreamworks, Universal that's just hanging ... I feel like they've got this big sword of Damocles hanging over their head and they're spending their time just doing the goofiest stuff they can imagine before that all comes due. It's great. It's fun.

Zoë Schiffer: They cannot be stopped. That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

He's the CEO of Palantir, basically making this a core issue for America winning the AI race. Palantir and Nvidia, they have a vested interest in pushing forward this plan. More AI, more systems mean more GPUs—that directly benefits Nvidia's bottom line. And Palantir is deploying AI systems on government systems and other places where security is really paramount and they need to do that on American technology, but it's much easier to do it with systems that you can tweak, play around with, modify, change.Brian Barrett: It is interesting these strange, not strange, but the way that the, I'm going to say battle lines, I don't mean that, it's too dramatic, but that they're being drawn, the sort of argument lines are being drawn in this. To your point, Nvidia's Jensen Huang spoke with Axios recently and he spelled out exactly why the proliferation of open models would benefit his company.Jensen Huang, archival audio: First of all, with great AI, open models, it's great for the whole industry. If there's great AI, even if it's open, wherever it comes from, there will be more use. Whenever there's more use, you'll have to sell a lot more Nvidia computers. We'll have to build more data centers, we'll have more services. The technology will diffuse into more industries. And so, starting point is great models lead to great use, which leads to great growth.Brian Barrett: And I think the counterpoint of that too is great disasters in the cybersecurity space leads to more regulation, leads to clamping down on AI, which hurts Nvidia's growth. So, the sort of let's have a security consortium, let's slow everybody's role here, is I think a protective play to say, let's avoid those sort of extreme moments that are going to cause a real crackdown on this industry and really slow the growth, on which, as we've said many times before, a big part of the US economy depends at this point.Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it's like you could see this moment where OpenAI's agents kind of go rogue as a moment where the US government does clamp down and says, "This is really scary. We need to slow growth." I think that the open weight, open source push is really an opportunity to say, "Actually, we need more growth. We need more investment, but we need it in this other area." And basically the idea is these attacks are going to keep happening, whether intentionally or not, and US companies need every possible tool at their disposal to defend themselves.Leah Feiger: So, kind of moving this to DC a little bit, I want to talk about all of the people that are involved with this kind of regulation right now. This week, Hugo published a really handy map on who's actually calling the shots on AI policy inside the Trump administration. It turns out it's not entirely a clear answer, and there's a couple of different influencing voices. And one senior official actually told Hugo, in one of my favorite quotes we've gotten in a while on this, "It's not an argument with two sides, it's an argument with 10 sides." So, the names that he's calling out here, you're not going to be super surprised, right? It's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. It's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. It's former AI Czar David Sacks. You have Arvind Raman, the acting director for Center for AI Standards and Innovation, who's Lutnick's top deputy there. It's a really, really interesting mix of people who all are trying very, very hard to get their own interests across. And from Hugo's reporting, it seems like Trump is listening to all of them.Zoë Schiffer: Can I ask, Leah, what do these different people, what side of the debate are they coming down on when we think about open source, closed source? What do they want right now?Leah Feiger: Everyone is kind of in different parts of this. I would say there's a very interesting split. Lutnick is trying right now, for example, to figure out ways to create incentives for US labs to just create their own open weight models to counterbalance China. He's not exactly taking a very, very harsh stance one way or the other. He's kind of straddling a middle ground on regulation. He imposed export controls on Anthropic famously, but he's been kind of freewheeling than others in the White House, which is sort of key here. So, if I'm an AI lab, I would be interested in having Lutnick's ear. And Hugo's reporting also found that he's been speaking to a number of leaders at AI Labs, so not hugely surprising there. And then on the other hand, you have national cyber director Sean Cairncross. He's taken a very hard line approach. He's had a huge role in attempts to regulate Chinese AI. He's pretty beloved as far as we can tell at the White House and has been working alongside some other folks to develop a policy to counter the potential national security risks of AI, especially from China. He was very involved in President Trump's June 2 executive order. Everyone's kind of trying to figure out what they want to say and how they want to pitch it to the president whose most consistent take here has been like, "We will not be stifling US innovation."Brian Barrett: China definitely seems to be a common thread here and makes sense as a lens to view your AI policy through in general because you've got this, if you see it as this is a race between the US and China, we can't lose. But that does position you, I think, to maybe miss some other aspects of what's going on here. I think especially in terms of US companies saying, "Hey, maybe we don't actually want to win this race quite as fast," or employees at companies saying that. I don't know. Curious what you think about what they may not be taking into account here if they're so focused on China as the prism through which all of their AI policy is kind of reflecting out or most of it.Leah Feiger: Such a good question. In so many ways, the Trump administration is focused on what is in front of their face at that moment in time. So, if the conversation of the week is China versus open weight versus US models versus all of these different conversations, that's what they're going to be weighing in on and also utilizing it to push some of their other positions. I'm thinking of Treasury Secretary Bessent who is very, very obsessed with distillation right now. He for sure has taken the most aggressive stance towards Chinese AI and its efforts to distill US models. But in a very public post on X last week talked about distillation as IP theft. He threatened Chinese labs with sanctions or inclusions on the entity list, this trade restriction list maintained by the US government. I guess all to say, these were already things that Bessent was really, really thinking about. So, now being able to apply it to the new lens is of course where he's heading. We're also kind of watching some people make their names in this right now, whether it's China or not. Someone that I'm very, very curious about on this list, not a household name by any means. The assistant secretary for financial institutions at the Treasury—say that five times fast—Luke Pettit, he has become the point person on AI at Treasury under Bessent. Who is this man? He was previously a senior policy adviser in the US Senate. And now you guys are going to enjoy this one: He's working alongside the Treasury's chief information officer and former DOGE member Sam Corcos.Brian Barrett: Oh, I remember Sam.Leah Feiger: Exactly. It's a fun reunion for all. It's this fascinating thing where people already had their preconceived, I'm kind of out here to blame China for a lot of regulatory issues. I'm out here to encourage US innovation. And then I'm out here to make a name for myself. How do you get involved in this? This is the topic of the moment. How do you make your mark?Zoë Schiffer: It's so interesting. The distillation thing was really catching my eye. We talked about Moonshot AI's latest model coming out K3, I think it's called, and these immediate allegations that they had distilled models from top US labs. And then I was really struck by multiple Kimi researchers on X making jokes being like, "Oh yeah, within two weeks we distilled Fable." That's not even technically possible. As usual, AI drama plays out on X. I mean, the thing about that is we do have very good evidence that Chinese AI labs were distilling US models. There were times where you would talk to those Chinese open models and they would respond as Claude. I think that that evidence is pretty sound. Whether they did it this time around, I'm not sure, but it does feel like the US government has gotten involved in this debate pretty late. It's like a lot of this has already happened. It's not to say they shouldn't take action necessarily, but I'm a little bit curious. One, technically speaking, how do you plan to do that? I mean, it doesn't seem like necessarily sanctioning the labs would be that effective in terms of distillation. And then two, is it genuinely too late or can you stop significant distillation or “IP theft” from happening going forward?Brian Barrett: I'll say though, I will say we have seen some movement even this week, right? The FCC has banned the import of foreign-made power inverter models, which is important for data center building. They've banned foreign-made humanoid robots, which is going to be huge. That's where China is leading the US. So, we haven't gotten to the point where they're doing other things, but they are taking steps and they do have some levers they can pull. I just want to add one more note on this whole conversation, which is we record this on Wednesday afternoon Eastern Time. And as we're talking now, Sam Altman is on Capitol Hill shaking hands, kissing babies, talking to senators, telling them why his AI models are good and not bad actually. So, we'll see if that turns into anything probably if they're just listening to the last voice they hear. Over the weekend, people were just surprised to discover that some chats that they had had with Claude could actually be found via search on the web. You could go to Google and you can search, put in a specific search term to find shared Claude chats, and it would show them back to you. You could go through several hundred of these at least. Google has been taking them down since then. But just to understand how this happened, basically Anthropic lets you share a Claude chat via what's known as a snapshot URL. It's basically if you want to share a specific conversation with somebody, it'll make a link for you and you can send that link to that person and they can look over it. It's not intended for public indexing, but Google basically ignored instructions that Anthropic had put on its sites and it was indexing these chats anyway. It's not a great thing. It's also not the first time this has happened. Google is blaming Anthropic saying that it's their fault, not theirs. So, there's a lot of messiness here too. While it may sound like, well, people were just sharing stuff, so they can't have been that private in the first place. Some of the stuff that was found in these chats includes erotic role-play. Some of it includes medical information being shared within a medical firm, right? So, "Hey, I've got this information about this patient." So, in that case, the person whose privacy is implicated had nothing to do with the chats in the first place other than being a patient at this place. So, some really private personal stuff in here.Leah Feiger: Did either of you see this news and get nervous for yourselves?Zoë Schiffer: Leah's looking right at me now. No, I don't—Leah Feiger: I was like, "Zoë, do you need to tell me something?"Zoë Schiffer: I know, I know. No, you would be the only person I would share such chats with, and I don't do that to you, to preserve our relationship. I've had people share their chats with me. Usually, it's sources being like, "I could explain it to you, but here's my conversation with Claude." And I'm like, "I think I would rather you just explain it to me." I mean, it's a little bit ironic, because who is very famous for ignoring the X robots tag header thingy that do not index this request? It's AI companies. So, the fact that it's now coming back to bite an AI company, a little bit ironic, a little bit funny. But I think it gets to this larger question around just the privacy of conversations with chatbots, which have been coming up in a variety of different ways, both cybersecurity related, legal, otherwise.Brian Barrett: Yeah. People famously have had chats treating their chatbots like a lawyer, and the chatbot has told them, "Hey, this is inadmissible because you're getting legal advice." And then it winds up in court because of course you cannot claim attorney-client privilege with Claude or ChatGPT.Zoë Schiffer: Did you guys read the New York magazine cover story a few weeks ago that was like, what if it all came out?Leah Feiger: I loved it. My group chat was absolutely alight. We started asking each other, "What have you asked recently?" I think I'm the only one that escapes from this doomsday universe.Zoë Schiffer: Leah's very like, "I have nothing to hide. Come at me, NSA."Leah Feiger: Nothing to hide. Go check my receipts. But yeah, big takeaway for users. Manage this yourselves. Don't forget that the robots surveil you. Settings. Go to settings, then privacy, then shared chats. You can change this. Coming up after the break, we'll be sharing our WIRED/TIRED pics of the week.Zoë Schiffer: All right, it's time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. In case you've forgotten whatever is new and cool is WIRED, whatever is uncool and lame and old is TIRED. Leah, what are yours for this week?Leah Feiger: My TIRED is zoo. I struggle with this. I have friends with kids who are like, "Say this aloud to me one more time. We're going to have an issue." And I totally understand that. It's an amazing way for people to engage with the natural world, but I'm always thinking about the animals. You're at a zoo, you're at the aquarium, and it's incredibly sad. I'm really using this TIRED, which seems fairly irrelevant in a news to bring you into my WIRED, which is actual news. And that might be that not all zoos are bad. This week, WIRED's Kate Knibbs reported on this unbelievable rescue mission that ended up saving four beluga whales from probable death. This all started because this notorious aquarium and theme park in Canada called Marineland went bankrupt back in 2024. It's been sitting around since. And last year, Marineland finally announced that they might have to euthanize these belugas if no one stepped in to help transfer them to a new facility.Zoë Schiffer: Oh my god, this is not where I thought that was going.Leah Feiger: No, really, really awful. And honestly, the drone footage of this basically turned me into the Joker last year. I just remember watching from above these belugas just kind of bouncing off walls. It was so upsetting, totally abandoned amusement park vibes. I thought it was AI. Anyway, really, really awful story. But it ends OK, or parts of it are beginning to end OK. This past week, a team from Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, shout out Chicago, pulled off truly a logistical marvel, putting four belugas into custom stretchers, loading them into individual saltwater tanks, trucking them to the airport, flying them across an international border on a chartered 777. The whole thing took 72 hours.Archival audio: A round of applause after a round-the-clock relocation effort. Shedd Aquarium staff have successfully moved four beluga whales from a facility in Niagara Falls, Ontario, to their new home.Zoë Schiffer: Is their new home better?Leah Feiger: I mean, their new home is not going to kill them? And also gives them food. But again, there's obviously still so much criticism of captivity for these large animals. I mean, everyone saw Blackfish. Everyone's aware of Tilikum, the really famous orca.Brian Barrett: Leah, you're going to hit, I know, Free Willy, and that's where my orca knowledge ends.Leah Feiger: This poor orca, who is this feature of this massive documentary about basically going crazy because these creatures are so, so smart and trapped in tanks and forced to perform tricks. So, very, very happy. The article is honestly very cool and interesting, and you were able to transport these creatures. But obviously, the slightly little sour note is these guys should be in the ocean. They should be hanging out. But that's still my WIRED.Brian Barrett: Go read Kate's story and also look at the photos in it because they're amazing.Zoë Schiffer: 100 percent. Brian.Brian Barrett: All right, here's my TIRED. Wait for it. Beep, beep, beep. That's my impression of a microwave beep letting you know that something's done. It's annoying. It's loud. It's repetitive. It's tired.Zoë Schiffer: I feel like I just got a glimpse of what you're like as a dad.Brian Barrett: Oh, just barely scratching the surface, Zoë. My WIRED is a couple of sound designers who have a startup called Starling, or a company called Starling, have made it their quest to design a better microwave beep. One that sounds pleasant, one that's not annoying, one that works with technology that's not too expensive. And it's really fascinating. Jeremy White, senior writer at WIRED, spent some time talking to these folks, has a really interesting dive into why microwaves and other kinds of tech, just like we sort of settle for annoyances when we don't necessarily have to. I think there's so many things that are just like, it's a little thing, but it could be better, but no one's bothered to make it better because it maybe costs 50 bucks to make it better. These guys are trying. And I think it's interesting. I think it's fun when people expect more from their technology. So, a fun story from Jeremy.Zoë Schiffer: I love that. I love that. I love taking a thing that's kind of vaguely annoying, but we've just accepted as part of life and then being like, "What if it was nice?"Leah Feiger: Yeah, that's lovely. Big fan.Brian Barrett: Yeah. OK, Zoë.Leah Feiger: Take it away.Zoë Schiffer: I'm going to loudly insert myself into this party. TIRED: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter, $10 billion, snore, heard it, whatever. WIRED is Midjourney, the AI image generator acquiring Co-Star, the astrology app. I was—Leah Feiger: So, funny.Zoë Schiffer: We don't know the terms of the deal. I'm waiting, someone tell me. But I just found this so funny. If you think about Midjourney at all, you've been thinking, what is this company up to? What is happening over there? They have talked about making a full-body scanner of sorts, some sort of physical, AI-powered product that they're going to put in spas, medical spas? Now they have this Co-Star thing going. The app has 4.3 million users. Now its CEO is going to be Midjourney's chief design officer. Midjourney hasn't had a consumer app, so maybe now they'll have one. They're apparently working on one. I just have so many questions. I was laughing when I read Mike Isaac's post about this on X. He said, "Could someone tell me why a generative AI company could buy an astrology app? Because I am not that smart." And I was like, "Me either, frankly. I don't know."Brian Barrett: But for some reason, I just love that this Midjourney's journey into medical scanners, fortunes is happening against this backdrop of they've been staring down one of the biggest IP lawsuits from Disney, 20th Century Fox, Dreamworks, Universal that's just hanging ... I feel like they've got this big sword of Damocles hanging over their head and they're spending their time just doing the goofiest stuff they can imagine before that all comes due. It's great. It's fun.Zoë Schiffer: They cannot be stopped. That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. blocks.html_en: Zoë Schiffer: Okay, you guys, we have to talk about this strange alliance that formed earlier this week. So, basically Nvidia announced was joining forces with more than 40 companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, Palantir, and IBM to launch something called the Open Secure AI Alliance. Really rolls off the tongue. The stated goal is basically to build and share open source tools for AI-powered cybersecurity defense. But it's really interesting because Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are not on the list. blocks.html_en: Brian Barrett: I'll say though, I will say we have seen some movement even this week, right? The FCC has banned the import of foreign-made power inverter models, which is important for data center building. They've banned foreign-made humanoid robots, which is going to be huge. That's where China is leading the US. So, we haven't gotten to the point where they're doing other things, but they are taking steps and they do have some levers they can pull. I just want to add one more note on this whole conversation, which is we record this on Wednesday afternoon Eastern Time. And as we're talking now, Sam Altman is on Capitol Hill shaking hands, kissing babies, talking to senators, telling them why his AI models are good and not bad actually. So, we'll see if that turns into anything probably if they're just listening to the last voice they hear. Over the weekend, people were just surprised to discover that some chats that they had had with Claude could actually be found via search on the web. You could go to Google and you can search, put in a specific search term to find shared Claude chats, and it would show them back to you. You could go through several hundred of these at least. Google has been taking them down since then. But just to understand how this happened, basically Anthropic lets you share a Claude chat via what's known as a snapshot URL. It's basically if you want to share a specific conversation with somebody, it'll make a link for you and you can send that link to that person and they can look over it. It's not intended for public indexing, but Google basically ignored instructions that Anthropic had put on its sites and it was indexing these chats anyway. It's not a great thing. It's also not the first time this has happened. Google is blaming Anthropic saying that it's their fault, not theirs. So, there's a lot of messiness here too. While it may sound like, well, people were just sharing stuff, so they can't have been that private in the first place. Some of the stuff that was found in these chats includes erotic role-play. Some of it includes medical information being shared within a medical firm, right? So, "Hey, I've got this information about this patient." So, in that case, the person whose privacy is implicated had nothing to do with the chats in the first place other than being a patient at this place. So, some really private personal stuff in here.

content_html_zh:
本周，该团队在《恐怖谷》节目中讨论了英伟达引人注目的联盟的成立，该联盟旨在与微软、SpaceX 和 Palantir 等公司一起推动开源人工智能安全。 明显缺席？ OpenAI 和 Anthropic。 Brian Barrett、Zoë Schiffer 和 Leah Feiger 详细分析了这种分裂对行业意味着什么，以及特朗普政府自己对人工智能的看法转变。 另外，我们还讨论了克劳德的对话如何出现在谷歌和必应的搜索结果中，以及如何营救四头鲸鱼并将其从加拿大运送到芝加哥的伟大壮举。

本期提到的文章：

  • 克劳德的私人聊天记录出现在 Google 和 Bing 搜索结果中
  • 硅谷对中国人工智能完全分裂
  • 特朗普政府因人工智能监管而自相矛盾
  • 带领 4 头白鲸前往芝加哥的野生救援任务内部
  • 系统更新通讯：《连线》精选

您可以通过 @brbarrett 关注 Bluesky 上的 Brian Barrett，@zoeschiffer 上关注 Bluesky 上的 Zoë Schiffer，@leahfeiger 上关注 Bluesky 上的 Leah Feiger。 请通过 [email protected] 给我们写信。

如何聆听

如果您使用的是 iPhone 或 iPad，请打开名为“播客”的应用程序，或者只需点击此链接。 您还可以下载 Overcast 或 Pocket Casts 等应用程序，然后搜索“恐怖谷”。 我们也在 Spotify 上。

成绩单

注意：这是一个自动记录，可能包含错误。

Zoë Schiffer：欢迎来到《连线》杂志的恐怖谷。 我是佐伊·希弗 (Zoë Schiffer)，特约编辑。

布莱恩·巴雷特：我是布莱恩·巴雷特，执行主编。

利亚·费格：我是政治和科学主任利亚·费格。

Zoë Schiffer：今天在节目中，我们将深入探讨开源与封闭人工智能的争论，这一争论在过去的一周已经完全席卷了硅谷。 周一，英伟达宣布将与包括微软、SpaceX、IBM 在内的众多公司联手构建和共享开源人工智能安全工具。 我们将讨论为什么它会升温，以及这是否可能成为人工智能在美国实际制造的拐点。

Leah Feiger：在白宫，特朗普政府官员对于人工智能的发展有一些不同的看法。 我们将讨论目前在人工智能政策方面影响特朗普政府的一些关键参与者，以及他们如何积极影响整个国家的对话。

Brian Barrett：我们还将详细分析为什么 Claude 聊天记录会在 Google 搜索和 Bing 搜索中曝光。 对于那些仍在使用 Bing 的人来说，您也身处其中。 出于有趣的原因，我们将深入探讨它。

Zoë Schiffer：好吧，你们，我们必须谈谈本周早些时候形成的这个奇怪的联盟。 因此，基本上 Nvidia 宣布将与包括 Microsoft、SpaceX、Palantir 和 IBM 在内的 40 多家公司联手推出名为“开放安全 AI 联盟”的组织。 真的是脱口而出。 既定目标基本上是为人工智能驱动的网络安全防御构建和共享开源工具。 但这确实很有趣，因为谷歌、OpenAI 和 Anthropic 都不在名单上。 这一消息是在上周发生的事件之后发布的，两名 OpenAI 代理在一次安全测试中基本上失控并破坏了人工智能平台 Hugging Face。 当英伟达宣布这个联盟时，他们实际上点名了这一事件并表示，“这清楚地提醒我们，网络防御者需要开放的前沿代理系统来进行自卫。” 这有点暴露了这场长期酝酿的争论，我们在播客上已经讨论过几次了，那就是，到目前为止，美国实际上已经在很大程度上放弃了开放权重和开源，转而全力投入专有系统，而现在这已经成为一个问题。

Brian Barrett：OpenAI 事件确实引发了许多相互交叉的问题。 你有开放式人工智能与封闭式人工智能，你有人工智能安全以及谁对此负责。 你有美国的监管。 现在甚至有超过 1100 名顶级情报公司的工作人员签署了一份请愿书，呼吁美国政府帮助有意识地加快“人工智能发展”速度，以防止其发展过快。 他们说：“请放慢我们的速度，因为事情已经有点失控了。” 最重要的是，事实证明 OpenAI 最初披露的情况甚至不是故事的全部。 周二晚上有消息称，其一名特工实际上闯入了四个不属于 Hugging Face 的不同平台，从而进入了 Hugging Face。 所以，这并不是什么意思，但它确实触及了人工智能世界中的许多热点，并使许多已经推迟了一段时间的对话达到了紧要关头。

佐伊·希弗：是的，我会说，看到你提到的那封大公开信，我感到非常惊讶。

档案音频：来自顶级人工智能公司的 1000 多名员工签署了一份请愿书，呼吁美国政府帮助“刻意加快人工智能的发展速度”。 公开信的签署人包括Anthropic首席执行官以及OpenAI和Meta超级智能实验室的首席科学家。

Zoë Schiffer：我的想法基本上是，我们没有从 Dario Amodei 的说法中学到任何东西，即人工智能真的很可怕和危险吗？ 然后，美国政府对人性化的询问非常严厉，你可能真的会收到，我不知道他们是否希望美国政府做他们能做的事情，如果他们从字面上听这封信，但这确实表明，即使是人们，我的意思是特别是从事人工智能系统工作的人也对种族正在做的事情感到害怕。

利亚·费格：是的，我的意思是，上周我们在谈论华盛顿特区的反应以及从白宫角度来看正在发生的事情时，确实讨论了很多这个问题。 我对这种分裂很好奇。 上周我们讨论了这在硅谷真正造成的裂痕，即开源与专有人工智能的想法。 毫无疑问，这确实触及了现在的每一个部门。

Zoë Schiffer：我想说的是，周六我和一群来自 DC、Thinking Machines 的人工智能说客一起参加了这次活动。 米拉·莫拉迪也在场，白宫的迈克尔·克拉西奥斯也在场。 我对他们在这种平行人工智能世界中的运作方式感到非常震惊，这与我在旧金山实地看到的情况不同。 他们谈论了很多关于开源与闭源的问题。 当我特别与工程师交谈时，我会说他们中的大多数人都尝试了很多开放模型，但他们仍然发现 Codex 和 Claude 代码、OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的编码模型要优越得多。 因此，尽管它们贵得多，但他们最终还是使用了它们。 亚历克斯·卡普早些时候在电视上谈到了这一点。 他是 Palantir 的首席执行官，基本上使这成为美国赢得人工智能竞赛的核心问题。 Palantir 和 Nvidia 都对推动这一计划有着既得利益。 更多的人工智能、更多的系统意味着更多的 GPU，这直接有利于 Nvidia 的盈利。 Palantir 正在政府系统和其他安全至关重要的地方部署人工智能系统，他们需要利用美国技术来做到这一点，但使用可以调整、使用、修改、改变的系统来做到这一点要容易得多。

布莱恩·巴雷特：这些奇怪的事情很有趣，并不奇怪，但我要说的是战线的方式，我并不是说，它太戏剧化了，而是它们正在被绘制，这种争论线正在被绘制出来。 就你的观点而言，Nvidia 的 Jensen Huang 最近与 Axios 进行了交谈，他详细说明了为什么开放模型的扩散将使他的公司受益。

Jensen Huang，档案音频：首先，拥有强大的人工智能、开放的模型，这对整个行业来说都是伟大的。 如果有伟大的人工智能，即使它是开放的，无论它来自哪里，都会有更多的用途。 每当使用量增加时，您就必须出售更多的 Nvidia 计算机。 我们将不得不建立更多的数据中心，我们将提供更多的服务。 该技术将扩散到更多行业。 因此，出发点是伟大的模型带来巨大的用途，从而带来巨大的增长。

Brian Barrett：我认为与之相反的是网络安全领域的巨大灾难会导致更多的监管，导致对人工智能的压制，这会损害英伟达的增长。 所以，让我们建立一个安全联盟，让我们放慢每个人在这里的角色，我认为这是一种保护性的游戏，让我们避免那种极端的时刻，这些时刻将导致对这个行业的真正打击并真正减缓增长，正如我们之前多次说过的那样，美国经济的很大一部分此时取决于这个行业。

Zoë Schiffer：是的，就好像你可以看到 OpenAI 的代理变得无赖的那一刻，就像美国政府确实采取严厉措施并说：“这真的很可怕。 我们需要放慢增长速度。” 我认为开放权重、开源推动确实是一个机会，可以说：“实际上，我们需要更多的增长。 我们需要更多投资，但我们需要在其他领域进行投资。” 基本上，我们的想法是，无论是有意还是无意，这些攻击都会不断发生，美国公司需要一切可能的工具来保护自己。

Leah Feiger：所以，稍微把这个问题转移到华盛顿特区，我想谈谈现在参与此类监管的所有人员。 本周，雨果发布了一张非常方便的地图，显示了特朗普政府内部人工智能政策的真正发号施令者。 事实证明，这并不完全是一个明确的答案，并且存在一些不同的影响声音。 一位高级官员实际上告诉雨果，这是我一段时间以来最喜欢的引言之一，“这不是两个方面的争论，而是十个方面的争论。” 所以，他在这里喊出的名字，你不会感到非常惊讶，对吧？ 我是商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克。 我是国家网络总监肖恩·凯恩克罗斯。 他是前人工智能沙皇大卫·萨克斯。 阿尔温德·拉曼 (Arvind Raman) 是人工智能标准与创新中心的代理主任，也是卢特尼克的最高副手。 这是一个非常非常有趣的人组合，他们都非常非常努力地表达自己的兴趣。 从雨果的报道来看，特朗普似乎正在倾听所有人的意见。

Zoë Schiffer：Leah，我可以问一下，当我们考虑开源和闭源时，这些不同的人会站在辩论的哪一边？ 他们现在想要什么？

Leah Feiger：每个人都处于不同的部分。 我想说这是一个非常有趣的分裂。 例如，卢特尼克现在正在尝试寻找方法来激励美国实验室创建自己的开放重量模型来制衡中国。 不管怎样，他并没有采取非常非常严厉的立场。 他在监管方面处于中间立场。 他对人类实施出口管制是出了名的，但他比白宫其他人更随心所欲，这是这里的关键。 所以，如果我是人工智能实验室，我会对 Lutnick 的耳朵感兴趣。 雨果的报告还发现，他一直在与人工智能实验室的一些领导者进行交谈，因此这并不令人感到惊讶。 另一方面，国家网络总监肖恩·凯恩克罗斯 (Sean Cairncross)。 他采取了非常强硬的态度。 他在监管中国人工智能方面发挥了巨大作用。 据我们所知，他在白宫非常受人爱戴，并且一直在与其他一些人一起制定一项政策，以应对人工智能潜在的国家安全风险，尤其是来自中国的风险。 他积极参与特朗普总统 6 月 2 日的行政命令。 每个人都在试图弄清楚他们想说什么，以及他们想如何向总统推销，而总统在这里最一贯的观点是，“我们不会扼杀美国的创新。”

布莱恩·巴雷特（Brian Barrett）：中国似乎绝对是这里的一个共同点，并且作为一个观察人工智能政策的镜头是有意义的，因为你已经明白了这一点，如果你认为这是美国和中国之间的一场竞赛，我们就不会输。 但我认为，这确实会让你错过这里发生的事情的其他一些方面。 我认为尤其是美国公司会说，“嘿，也许我们实际上并不想那么快赢得这场比赛”，或者公司的员工会这么说。 我不知道。 很好奇你怎么想，如果他们如此关注中国，将其作为他们所有或大部分人工智能政策的棱镜，那么他们在这里可能没有考虑到什么。

利亚·费格：这是个好问题。 在很多方面，特朗普政府都专注于当时摆在他们面前的事情。 因此，如果本周的对话是中国与公开重量与美国模式与所有这些不同的对话，那么他们将对此进行权衡，并利用它来推动他们的一些其他立场。 我想到了财政部长贝森特，他现在非常非常痴迷于蒸馏。 他肯定对中国人工智能及其提炼美国模型的努力采取了最积极的立场。 但上周在 X 上的一篇非常公开的帖子中，将蒸馏视为知识产权盗窃。 他威胁要对中国实验室实施制裁或将其列入实体清单，该清单由美国政府维护。 我想总而言之，这些已经是贝森特真正、真正考虑过的事情了。 因此，现在能够将其应用到新镜头上当然是他的目标。 我们现在也看到一些人在这方面成名，无论是不是中国。 我对这个名单上的一个人非常非常好奇，无论如何，他并不是一个家喻户晓的名字。 财政部负责金融机构的助理部长卢克·佩蒂特（Luke Pettit）说得快了五倍，他已经成为贝森特领导下财政部人工智能方面的关键人物。 这个人是谁？ 他此前曾担任美国参议院高级政策顾问。 现在你们会喜欢这个：他与财政部首席信息官、前 DOGE 成员 Sam Corcos 一起工作。

布莱恩·巴雷特：哦，我记得萨姆。
